ERISA SECTION 510 — DISCHARGE OR DISCRIMINATION TO INTERFERE WITH EMPLOYEE-BENEFIT RIGHTS (29 U.S.C. § 1140) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ERISA SECTION 510 BENEFIT-INTERFERENCE RULE — APPLICABILITY NOTE
Section 510 of the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), codified at 29 U.S.C. § 1140, makes it unlawful to discharge, fine, suspend, expel, discipline, or discriminate against a participant or beneficiary of an employee benefit plan either for exercising a right under the plan or for the purpose of interfering with the attainment of a right the participant may become entitled to under the plan. This concerns Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc., recorded here as ending on October 1, 2026. The rule described in the information that follows applies only where an "employee benefit plan" within the meaning of ERISA is involved and only where the challenged action was taken with the purpose the statute describes; whether Acme, Inc. sponsors such a plan, whether Jordan Lee was a participant or beneficiary in it, and what motivated the separation on October 1, 2026 are all facts this sheet does not determine. Naming Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. here does not itself establish that any provision of ERISA applies to their relationship, and this sheet states what the statute and the courts have said rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular separation.

THE TWO PROHIBITIONS OF ERISA SECTION 510: RETALIATION FOR EXERCISING A PLAN RIGHT, AND INTERFERENCE WITH ATTAINING ONE
ERISA section 510, codified at 29 U.S.C. § 1140, makes it unlawful for "any person" to discharge, fine, suspend, expel, discipline, or discriminate against a participant or beneficiary of an employee benefit plan on two distinct grounds. The first is retaliatory: acting against the participant or beneficiary "for exercising any right to which he is entitled" under the plan, under ERISA's Title I, or under the other statutes the section lists. The second is anticipatory: acting "for the purpose of interfering with the attainment of any right to which such participant may become entitled" under the plan or under ERISA's Title I. The prohibition is not limited to the employer that sponsors the plan — it reaches "any person" — and the list of forbidden acts extends beyond discharge to fines, suspensions, expulsions, discipline, and discrimination. Under the second prong, the wrong lies in the purpose behind the adverse action, not merely in the fact that a benefit right was lost; that element is the subject of a separate clause in this document. As applied to Jordan Lee's separation from Acme, Inc. on October 1, 2026, this clause states what the statute prohibits, not whether that separation falls within it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "It shall be unlawful for any person to discharge, fine, suspend, expel, discipline, or discriminate against a participant or beneficiary for exercising any right to which he is entitled under the provisions of an employee benefit plan, this subchapter, section 1201 of this title, or the Welfare and Pension Plans Disclosure Act [29 U.S.C. 301 et seq.], or for the purpose of interfering with the attainment of any right to which such participant may become entitled under the plan, this subchapter, or the Welfare and Pension Plans Disclosure Act."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1140 (ERISA § 510) — Interference with protected rights (first sentence), 29 U.S.C. § 1140 (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title29-section1140&num=0&edition=prelim)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory text (29 U.S.C. § 1140, first sentence), used as real evidence of the two prohibitions ERISA section 510 itself states — not a claim that any particular employer, plan, or separation falls within it, and not a determination that any adverse action was taken with the purpose the statute describes. The statute conditions its protection on the person being a "participant or beneficiary" of an "employee benefit plan"; this clause does not independently fetch or quote ERISA's definitions of those terms (29 U.S.C. § 1002) or ERISA's coverage and exemption provisions (29 U.S.C. §§ 1003, 1051), which determine whether a given arrangement is a covered plan at all — for example, governmental and church plans are generally outside Title I. The quoted sentence's cross-references to "section 1201 of this title" and the repealed Welfare and Pension Plans Disclosure Act are reproduced as they appear in the statute but not separately explained. Quote verification note: both fetched copies of the statute (uscode.house.gov and Cornell LII) carry stray spaces before some commas and inside the bracketed cross-reference where hyperlink tags were stripped (e.g., "section 1201 of this title ," and "[ 29 U.S.C. 301 et seq. ]"); the quote below reproduces the statute's punctuation without those artifacts, and the comparison was made after normalizing whitespace adjacent to punctuation and brackets.

PROTECTION FOR GIVING INFORMATION OR TESTIFYING, AND THE CROSS-REFERENCE TO ERISA'S CIVIL ENFORCEMENT SECTION
Section 510's second sentence states a separate prohibition that is not limited to plan participants and beneficiaries: it is unlawful to discharge, fine, suspend, expel, or discriminate against "any person" because that person has given information, has testified, or is about to testify in any inquiry or proceeding relating to ERISA or the Welfare and Pension Plans Disclosure Act. The section's final sentence then states that the provisions of 29 U.S.C. § 1132 — ERISA section 502, the statute's civil enforcement section — apply in enforcing section 510. Section 510 therefore describes prohibited conduct but does not itself create a freestanding remedy; the remedies, the court in which a claim is heard, and the availability of attorney's fees are all supplied by section 502, which is the subject of a later clause in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "It shall be unlawful for any person to discharge, fine, suspend, expel, or discriminate against any person because he has given information or has testified or is about to testify in any inquiry or proceeding relating to this chapter or the Welfare and Pension Plans Disclosure Act."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1140 (ERISA § 510) — protection for giving information or testifying (second sentence), 29 U.S.C. § 1140 (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title29-section1140&num=0&edition=prelim)
  "The provisions of section 1132 of this title shall be applicable in the enforcement of this section."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1140 (ERISA § 510) — enforcement cross-reference (final sentence), 29 U.S.C. § 1140 (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title29-section1140&num=0&edition=prelim)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory text (29 U.S.C. § 1140, second and fourth sentences), used as real evidence of the section's own witness/informant protection and of its express cross-reference to ERISA section 502 for enforcement — not a claim that any particular person gave information or testified in a covered inquiry or proceeding, and not a determination of what remedy would be available on any particular set of facts. The section's third sentence, concerning discrimination against a contributing employer to a multiemployer plan, is omitted here as outside the scope of an individual employee's separation. This clause does not independently establish what counts as an "inquiry or proceeding relating to this chapter," a question the statute does not define and this document does not resolve.

SECTION 510 PROTECTS NON-VESTED WELFARE BENEFITS (SUCH AS HEALTH COVERAGE), NOT ONLY PENSION VESTING
In Inter-Modal Rail Employees Assn. v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co. (1997), a unanimous United States Supreme Court rejected the Ninth Circuit's view that section 510 prohibits interference only with rights capable of "vesting" under ERISA. The case arose in Los Angeles: workers at a rail yard lost their railroad-retirement, pension, health, and welfare benefits when the railroad put their work out to bid and a lower-benefit contractor won it. The Ninth Circuit had allowed the workers' claim as to pension benefits but dismissed it as to health and welfare benefits on the theory that welfare benefits never vest and so no present "right" to them exists. The Supreme Court held that this reading is contradicted by the statute's plain language: because ERISA defines a "plan" to include a welfare benefit plan, and because welfare plans by design offer benefits that do not vest, Congress's use of the word "plan" — rather than "pension plan" or "nonforfeitable right" — forecloses confining section 510 to vested rights. The Court acknowledged that an employer generally remains free to amend or terminate a welfare plan through the plan's formal amendment procedures, but held that this power does not include the power to discharge or discriminate against individual participants for the purpose of interfering with their attainment of plan rights, because otherwise employers could "informally" amend plans one participant at a time. In short, the Court said, section 510 exists to ensure that employers do not circumvent the provision of promised benefits.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "The Court of Appeals’ holding that § 510 bars interference only with vested rights is contradicted by the plain language of § 510."
  — Inter-Modal Rail Employees Assn. v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co., 520 U.S. 510 (1997) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/118108/inter-modal-rail-employees-assn-v-atchison-topeka-santa-fe-railway-co/)
  "Because a “plan” includes an “employee welfare benefit plan,” and because welfare plans offer benefits that do not “vest” (at least insofar as ERISA is concerned), Congress’ use of the word “plan” in §510 all but forecloses the argument"
  — Inter-Modal Rail Employees Assn. v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co., 520 U.S. 510 (1997) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/118108/inter-modal-rail-employees-assn-v-atchison-topeka-santa-fe-railway-co/)
  "But §510 draws no distinction between those rights that “vest” under ERISA and those that do not."
  — Inter-Modal Rail Employees Assn. v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co., 520 U.S. 510 (1997) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/118108/inter-modal-rail-employees-assn-v-atchison-topeka-santa-fe-railway-co/)
  "The formal amendment process would be undermined if §510 did not apply because employers could “informally” amend their plans one participant at a time."
  — Inter-Modal Rail Employees Assn. v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co., 520 U.S. 510 (1997) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/118108/inter-modal-rail-employees-assn-v-atchison-topeka-santa-fe-railway-co/)
  Known gap: This is a United States Supreme Court decision (Inter-Modal Rail Employees Assn. v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Ry. Co., 520 U.S. 510 (1997)), used as real evidence that section 510's interference clause covers non-vested welfare benefits as well as pension rights — not a claim that any particular loss of health or other welfare coverage at a separation resulted from a prohibited purpose. The Court vacated and remanded without deciding the case on its facts; in particular, it expressly left for the Court of Appeals the employer's alternative argument that section 510 protects only an employee's crossing of the "threshold of eligibility" for welfare benefits, so this clause does not state how that argument was ultimately resolved. The opinion's typography differs between the two fetched sources (Cornell LII renders the section symbol as "§510" without a space and uses straight quotation marks; the CourtListener text uses "§ 510" and typographic quotation marks); quotes below follow the CourtListener text, and the comparison against the Cornell copy was made after normalizing section-symbol spacing and quotation-mark style.

THE EMPLOYER'S PURPOSE IS THE ELEMENT: SPECIFIC INTENT TO INTERFERE, NOT AN INCIDENTAL LOSS OF BENEFITS
Section 510's interference prong turns on why the adverse action was taken. The Ninth Circuit — whose decisions bind the federal courts sitting in California — stated the element in Dytrt v. Mountain State Telephone & Telegraph Co. (1990): a claimant must show that employment was terminated because of a specific intent to interfere with ERISA rights, and no action lies where the loss of rights is merely a consequence of the termination rather than a motivating factor behind it. In that case a long-tenured manager whose position was eliminated elected an early-retirement program and then tried to withdraw the election; the court held that the fact her pension would have been larger had she stayed employed was an incidental effect of the employer's refusal to let her revoke, not a motivating factor, and affirmed judgment against her on the section 510 claim (while reversing on a separate fiduciary-duty claim). The Supreme Court made the same point in Inter-Modal (1997): when an employer acts without the purpose of interfering with plan rights, as can be the case when it makes fundamental business decisions, its actions are not barred by section 510. Almost every discharge reduces or ends some benefit; section 510 is concerned with discharges undertaken in order to bring that about.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "A claimant must show that employment was terminated because of a specific intent to interfere with ERISA rights in order to prevail under § 510; no action lies where the alleged loss of rights is a mere consequence, as opposed to a motivating factor behind the termination."
  — Dytrt v. Mountain State Telephone & Telegraph Co., 921 F.2d 889 (9th Cir. 1990) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/553262/barbara-a-dytrt-v-the-mountain-state-telephone-and-telegraph-company/)
  "This was an incidental effect, and not a motivating factor of the Plan Review Committee’s decision to deny Dytrt’s request for revocation of her acceptance of retirement."
  — Dytrt v. Mountain State Telephone & Telegraph Co., 921 F.2d 889 (9th Cir. 1990) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/553262/barbara-a-dytrt-v-the-mountain-state-telephone-and-telegraph-company/)
  "To be sure, when an employer acts without this purpose, as could be the case when making fundamental business decisions, such actions are not barred by §510."
  — Inter-Modal Rail Employees Assn. v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway Co., 520 U.S. 510 (1997) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/118108/inter-modal-rail-employees-assn-v-atchison-topeka-santa-fe-railway-co/)
  Known gap: This is a Ninth Circuit decision (Dytrt v. Mountain State Telephone & Telegraph Co., 921 F.2d 889 (9th Cir. 1990)) together with a sentence of the Supreme Court's Inter-Modal opinion, used as real evidence that specific intent to interfere is an element of a section 510 interference claim and that an incidental benefit loss does not satisfy it — not a claim about what motivated any particular employer, and not a determination that any particular separation was or was not undertaken for a prohibited purpose. Dytrt concerned a refusal to let an employee revoke an early-retirement election rather than a conventional firing, and the Ninth Circuit drew its statement of the element from its earlier decision in Kimbro v. Atlantic Richfield Co., 889 F.2d 869 (9th Cir. 1989), which this clause does not independently fetch or quote. This clause does not describe how courts allocate the burden of proving intent (for example, whether the burden-shifting framework used in employment-discrimination cases applies), what circumstantial evidence has been found sufficient, or whether a benefit-cost motive that is one of several reasons for a discharge suffices — questions the quoted passages do not resolve. CourtListener's case-name field renders the employer as "Mountain State"; the opinion text itself refers to "The Mountain States Telephone and Telegraph Company."

A STATE-LAW WRONGFUL-DISCHARGE CLAIM PREMISED ON BENEFIT INTERFERENCE IS PREEMPTED; ERISA'S OWN REMEDY IS EXCLUSIVE
A California employee who believes a discharge was motivated by a desire to avoid benefit obligations cannot generally reframe that grievance as a state-law claim. In Ingersoll-Rand Co. v. McClendon (1990), the Supreme Court held that a state common-law wrongful-discharge claim alleging that an employee was fired to prevent his pension from vesting is preempted by ERISA. The Court reasoned first that such a claim "relates to" an ERISA plan under ERISA's express preemption clause (section 514(a)), because to prevail a plaintiff must plead, and the court must find, that a plan exists and that the employer had a pension-defeating motive. It reasoned second, and independently, that the state claim conflicts directly with section 510 itself — the claim is "prototypical" of what Congress meant section 510 to cover — and that ERISA section 502(a) is the exclusive remedy for section 510 rights, so that a plaintiff may not use state law to obtain remedies (there, lost wages, mental-anguish damages, and punitive damages) that Congress chose not to provide. The Court added that a plaintiff cannot avoid preemption by disclaiming any request for pension benefits. The Ninth Circuit had already reached the same result for California claims; the Supreme Court cited its Sorosky v. Burroughs Corp. decision among the courts holding such state wrongful-discharge actions preempted, and in Dytrt the Ninth Circuit stated that ERISA preempts implied-in-fact contract and implied-covenant-of-good-faith claims that duplicate an ERISA claim.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Thus, in order to prevail, a plaintiff must plead, and the court must find, that an ERISA plan exists and the employer had a pension-defeating motive in terminating the employment. Because the court’s inquiry must be directed to the plan, this judicially created cause of action “relate[s] to” an ERISA plan."
  — Ingersoll-Rand Co. v. McClendon, 498 U.S. 133 (1990) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/112512/ingersoll-rand-co-v-mcclendon/)
  "Congress viewed this section as a crucial part of ERISA because, without it, employers would be able to circumvent the provision of promised benefits."
  — Ingersoll-Rand Co. v. McClendon, 498 U.S. 133 (1990) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/112512/ingersoll-rand-co-v-mcclendon/)
  "Not only is § 502(a) the exclusive remedy for vindicating § 510-protected rights"
  — Ingersoll-Rand Co. v. McClendon, 498 U.S. 133 (1990) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/112512/ingersoll-rand-co-v-mcclendon/)
  "It is clear that the relief requested here is well within the power of federal courts to provide. Consequently, it is no answer to a pre-emption argument that a particular plaintiff is not seeking recovery of pension benefits."
  — Ingersoll-Rand Co. v. McClendon, 498 U.S. 133 (1990) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/112512/ingersoll-rand-co-v-mcclendon/)
  "(ERISA pre-empts state wrongful discharge actions premised on employer interference with the attainment of rights under employee benefit plans)"
  — Ingersoll-Rand Co. v. McClendon (footnote characterizing Sorosky v. Burroughs Corp., 826 F.2d 794 (9th Cir. 1987)), 498 U.S. 133 (1990) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/112512/ingersoll-rand-co-v-mcclendon/)
  "This Circuit has specifically held that ERISA preempts common law theories of breach of contract implied-in-fact, as well as state claims for breach of implied covenants of good faith and fair dealing (promises implied-in-law)."
  — Dytrt v. Mountain State Telephone & Telegraph Co., 921 F.2d 889 (9th Cir. 1990) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/553262/barbara-a-dytrt-v-the-mountain-state-telephone-and-telegraph-company/)
  Known gap: This is a United States Supreme Court decision (Ingersoll-Rand Co. v. McClendon, 498 U.S. 133 (1990)), supported by a sentence of the Ninth Circuit's Dytrt opinion, used as real evidence that a state-law discharge claim premised on benefit interference is preempted and that section 502(a) is the exclusive remedy for section 510 rights — not a claim about which theories are or are not available on any particular set of facts, and not a determination that every state-law claim arising from a separation that also affects benefits is preempted. Ingersoll-Rand involved a Texas common-law claim; the Ninth Circuit's Sorosky decision (826 F.2d 794 (9th Cir. 1987)) is referenced here only as the Supreme Court characterized it in a footnote and was not independently fetched or quoted. Preemption under section 514(a) has its own limits, which the Court acknowledged (state laws of general application that function irrespective of an ERISA plan, and laws that do not relate to an ongoing plan), and later Supreme Court decisions have refined the "relate to" inquiry; this clause does not survey that later case law. It also does not address whether a California statutory claim that does not depend on the existence of a plan (for example, a discrimination claim under the Fair Employment and Housing Act on a protected-characteristic theory) would be preempted — a distinct question the quoted passages do not decide. Quote verification note: the CourtListener text (from the U.S. Reports) and the Cornell LII text (from the slip opinion) differ in the typesetting of section symbols ("§ 510" versus "510" with no symbol) and in quotation-mark style; quotes below follow the CourtListener text, and comparison against the Cornell copy was made after removing section symbols and normalizing quotation marks. One genuine wording difference between the two copies was found and is disclosed here: in the sentence beginning "Not only is § 502(a) the exclusive remedy," the U.S. Reports text on CourtListener reads "rights, but there is no basis," while the Cornell slip-opinion text reads "rights, there is no basis" (no "but"); the quotation was accordingly cut to the clause that is identical in both copies, and the following two sentences, which are identical in both, are quoted separately.

HOW A SECTION 510 CLAIM IS ENFORCED: EQUITABLE RELIEF UNDER SECTION 502(A)(3), EXCLUSIVE FEDERAL JURISDICTION, AND DISCRETIONARY ATTORNEY'S FEES
Because section 510 directs that ERISA section 502 governs its enforcement, the shape of a section 510 claim is set by 29 U.S.C. § 1132. Under section 502(a)(3), a participant, beneficiary, or fiduciary may bring a civil action to enjoin any act or practice that violates ERISA or the plan's terms, or to obtain "other appropriate equitable relief" to redress such violations or to enforce ERISA or the plan. Under section 502(e)(1), the federal district courts have exclusive jurisdiction over such actions — the concurrent state-court jurisdiction ERISA allows for ordinary benefit-recovery claims under section 502(a)(1)(B) does not extend to a section 510 claim brought under section 502(a)(3). Under section 502(g)(1), in any such action the court "in its discretion may allow a reasonable attorney's fee and costs of action to either party" — a two-way, discretionary provision rather than an automatic award to a prevailing employee. The Supreme Court in Ingersoll-Rand relied on precisely these provisions in describing section 502(a) as a carefully integrated enforcement scheme whose remedies are exclusive.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "by a participant, beneficiary, or fiduciary (A) to enjoin any act or practice which violates any provision of this subchapter or the terms of the plan, or (B) to obtain other appropriate equitable relief (i) to redress such violations or (ii) to enforce any provisions of this subchapter or the terms of the plan;"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(3) (ERISA § 502(a)(3)) — civil action for injunctive or other appropriate equitable relief, 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(3) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title29-section1132&num=0&edition=prelim)
  "Except for actions under subsection (a)(1)(B) of this section, the district courts of the United States shall have exclusive jurisdiction of civil actions under this subchapter brought by the Secretary or by a participant, beneficiary, fiduciary, or any person referred to in section 1021(f)(1) of this title. State courts of competent jurisdiction and district courts of the United States shall have concurrent jurisdiction of actions under paragraphs (1)(B) and (7) of subsection (a) of this section."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1132(e)(1) (ERISA § 502(e)(1)) — exclusive federal jurisdiction, 29 U.S.C. § 1132(e)(1) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title29-section1132&num=0&edition=prelim)
  "In any action under this subchapter (other than an action described in paragraph (2)) by a participant, beneficiary, or fiduciary, the court in its discretion may allow a reasonable attorney's fee and costs of action to either party."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1132(g)(1) (ERISA § 502(g)(1)) — attorney's fees and costs, 29 U.S.C. § 1132(g)(1) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title29-section1132&num=0&edition=prelim)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory text (29 U.S.C. § 1132, subdivisions (a)(3), (e)(1), and (g)(1)), used as real evidence of who may sue under section 502(a)(3), the kind of relief that subdivision names, which courts hear such claims, and the fee provision — not a claim about what relief would be available or awarded on any particular set of facts. The statutory phrase "other appropriate equitable relief" has been the subject of extensive Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit case law on which remedies (for example, reinstatement, back pay, or monetary make-whole relief) qualify as "equitable," and on whether a jury trial is available; this clause does not fetch or summarize that case law and does not resolve those questions. ERISA section 510 contains no limitations period of its own, and federal courts have borrowed the most analogous state limitations period for section 510 claims; that borrowing rule and the resulting deadline in California are not independently verified here and are outside this clause's scope. The Ninth Circuit had allowed the workers' claim as to pension benefits but dismissed it as to health and welfare benefits on the theory that welfare benefits never vest and so no present "right" to them exists. The Supreme Court held that this reading is contradicted by the statute's plain language: because ERISA defines a "plan" to include a welfare benefit plan, and because welfare plans by design offer benefits that do not vest, Congress's use of the word "plan" — rather than "pension plan" or "nonforfeitable right" — forecloses confining section 510 to vested rights. The Court acknowledged that an employer generally remains free to amend or terminate a welfare plan through the plan's formal amendment procedures, but held that this power does not include the power to discharge or discriminate against individual participants for the purpose of interfering with their attainment of plan rights, because otherwise employers could "informally" amend plans one participant at a time. In short, the Court said, section 510 exists to ensure that employers do not circumvent the provision of promised benefits.

expectedJSON.body: Section 510's interference prong turns on why the adverse action was taken. The Ninth Circuit — whose decisions bind the federal courts sitting in California — stated the element in Dytrt v. Mountain State Telephone & Telegraph Co. (1990): a claimant must show that employment was terminated because of a specific intent to interfere with ERISA rights, and no action lies where the loss of rights is merely a consequence of the termination rather than a motivating factor behind it. In that case a long-tenured manager whose position was eliminated elected an early-retirement program and then tried to withdraw the election; the court held that the fact her pension would have been larger had she stayed employed was an incidental effect of the employer's refusal to let her revoke, not a motivating factor, and affirmed judgment against her on the section 510 claim (while reversing on a separate fiduciary-duty claim). The Supreme Court made the same point in Inter-Modal (1997): when an employer acts without the purpose of interfering with plan rights, as can be the case when it makes fundamental business decisions, its actions are not barred by section 510. Almost every discharge reduces or ends some benefit; section 510 is concerned with discharges undertaken in order to bring that about.

expectedJSON.body: A California employee who believes a discharge was motivated by a desire to avoid benefit obligations cannot generally reframe that grievance as a state-law claim. In Ingersoll-Rand Co. v. McClendon (1990), the Supreme Court held that a state common-law wrongful-discharge claim alleging that an employee was fired to prevent his pension from vesting is preempted by ERISA. The Court reasoned first that such a claim "relates to" an ERISA plan under ERISA's express preemption clause (section 514(a)), because to prevail a plaintiff must plead, and the court must find, that a plan exists and that the employer had a pension-defeating motive. It reasoned second, and independently, that the state claim conflicts directly with section 510 itself — the claim is "prototypical" of what Congress meant section 510 to cover — and that ERISA section 502(a) is the exclusive remedy for section 510 rights, so that a plaintiff may not use state law to obtain remedies (there, lost wages, mental-anguish damages, and punitive damages) that Congress chose not to provide. The Court added that a plaintiff cannot avoid preemption by disclaiming any request for pension benefits. The Ninth Circuit had already reached the same result for California claims; the Supreme Court cited its Sorosky v. Burroughs Corp. decision among the courts holding such state wrongful-discharge actions preempted, and in Dytrt the Ninth Circuit stated that ERISA preempts implied-in-fact contract and implied-covenant-of-good-faith claims that duplicate an ERISA claim.

citations.quote: Thus, in order to prevail, a plaintiff must plead, and the court must find, that an ERISA plan exists and the employer had a pension-defeating motive in terminating the employment. Because the court’s inquiry must be directed to the plan, this judicially created cause of action “relate[s] to” an ERISA plan.
Congress viewed this section as a crucial part of ERISA because, without it, employers would be able to circumvent the provision of promised benefits.
Not only is § 502(a) the exclusive remedy for vindicating § 510-protected rights

It is clear that the relief requested here is well within the power of federal courts to provide. Consequently, it is no answer to a pre-emption argument that a particular plaintiff is not seeking recovery of pension benefits.

McClendon, 498 U.S. 133 (1990)), supported by a sentence of the Ninth Circuit's Dytrt opinion, used as real evidence that a state-law discharge claim premised on benefit interference is preempted and that section 502(a) is the exclusive remedy for section 510 rights — not a claim about which theories are or are not available on any particular set of facts, and not a determination that every state-law claim arising from a separation that also affects benefits is preempted. Ingersoll-Rand involved a Texas common-law claim; the Ninth Circuit's Sorosky decision (826 F.2d 794 (9th Cir. 1987)) is referenced here only as the Supreme Court characterized it in a footnote and was not independently fetched or quoted. Preemption under section 514(a) has its own limits, which the Court acknowledged (state laws of general application that function irrespective of an ERISA plan, and laws that do not relate to an ongoing plan), and later Supreme Court decisions have refined the "relate to" inquiry; this clause does not survey that later case law. It also does not address whether a California statutory claim that does not depend on the existence of a plan (for example, a discrimination claim under the Fair Employment and Housing Act on a protected-characteristic theory) would be preempted — a distinct question the quoted passages do not decide. expectedJSON.body: Because section 510 directs that ERISA section 502 governs its enforcement, the shape of a section 510 claim is set by 29 U.S.C. § 1132. Under section 502(a)(3), a participant, beneficiary, or fiduciary may bring a civil action to enjoin any act or practice that violates ERISA or the plan's terms, or to obtain "other appropriate equitable relief" to redress such violations or to enforce ERISA or the plan. Under section 502(e)(1), the federal district courts have exclusive jurisdiction over such actions — the concurrent state-court jurisdiction ERISA allows for ordinary benefit-recovery claims under section 502(a)(1)(B) does not extend to a section 510 claim brought under section 502(a)(3). Under section 502(g)(1), in any such action the court "in its discretion may allow a reasonable attorney's fee and costs of action to either party" — a two-way, discretionary provision rather than an automatic award to a prevailing employee. The Supreme Court in Ingersoll-Rand relied on precisely these provisions in describing section 502(a) as a carefully integrated enforcement scheme whose remedies are exclusive.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(3) (ERISA § 502(a)(3)) — civil action for injunctive or other appropriate equitable relief
citations.quote: by a participant, beneficiary, or fiduciary (A) to enjoin any act or practice which violates any provision of this subchapter or the terms of the plan, or (B) to obtain other appropriate equitable relief (i) to redress such violations or (ii) to enforce any provisions of this subchapter or the terms of the plan;

Except for actions under subsection (a)(1)(B) of this section, the district courts of the United States shall have exclusive jurisdiction of civil actions under this subchapter brought by the Secretary or by a participant, beneficiary, fiduciary, or any person referred to in section 1021(f)(1) of this title. State courts of competent jurisdiction and district courts of the United States shall have concurrent jurisdiction of actions under paragraphs (1)(B) and (7) of subsection (a) of this section.

In any action under this subchapter (other than an action described in paragraph (2)) by a participant, beneficiary, or fiduciary, the court in its discretion may allow a reasonable attorney's fee and costs of action to either party.

expectedJSON.gap: This is federal statutory text (29 U.S.C. § 1132, subdivisions (a)(3), (e)(1), and (g)(1)), used as real evidence of who may sue under section 502(a)(3), the kind of relief that subdivision names, which courts hear such claims, and the fee provision — not a claim about what relief would be available or awarded on any particular set of facts. The statutory phrase "other appropriate equitable relief" has been the subject of extensive Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit case law on which remedies (for example, reinstatement, back pay, or monetary make-whole relief) qualify as "equitable," and on whether a jury trial is available; this clause does not fetch or summarize that case law and does not resolve those questions. ERISA section 510 contains no limitations period of its own, and federal courts have borrowed the most analogous state limitations period for section 510 claims; that borrowing rule and the resulting deadline in California are not independently verified here and are outside this clause's scope.
